key_finding: NIS-Agent reduces token cost by 33% versus baseline while matching or exceeding it on GAIA, WebWalkerQA, BrowseComp and BrowseComp-zh, by isolating context at webpage-triage and answer-validation decision points to counter a newly identified 'inertia bias'.
methodology: Introduces the IBIS benchmark, which controls search observations to isolate whether an agent is judging the outcome of its own prior action; evaluates the NIS-Agent context-isolation framework and a purpose-trained 8B model.
why_it_matters: Names and fixes a specific bias mechanism inside agentic search loops (self-authored action history distorting later judgment), giving a concrete architectural move — isolating triage from validation context — that a literature-search agent design should adopt or test against.
limitations: Evaluated on general web/QA deep-research benchmarks (GAIA, BrowseComp) rather than scientific-literature corpora
No comparison to a single-query database-search baseline
relevance_reason: Identifies and fixes a specific bias mechanism inside agentic search loops, directly informing agentic-mechanism design (decision 2).

key_finding: Search effort and answer quality are only weakly aligned; cumulative retrieval recall predicts accuracy far better than the number of searches, useful evidence often appears early yet agents keep searching, and the best-performing agents issue far fewer redundant queries.
methodology: Trajectory-level diagnosis with human-annotated document relevance judgments across six agents on BrowseComp-Plus, validated on BrowseComp via an open-web search API; decomposes failures into retrieval gaps versus utilization gaps.
why_it_matters: Directly undercuts the assumption that more iterative agentic search yields more gain: the diagnostic method (recall vs. iteration-count decomposition) transfers straight to evaluating any long-horizon literature-search agent and reframes decision 2/4 around stopping criteria and evidence quality rather than search volume.
limitations: Fixed retrieval model/harness limits generalization to other retrievers
BrowseComp-Plus/BrowseComp queries are general knowledge tasks, not scientific-literature search specifically
relevance_reason: Directly diagnoses which agentic behaviors carry gains and shows raw search effort does not, addressing the brief's decisions 2 and 4.

key_finding: Even leading deep-research systems (Gemini DR, OpenAI DR) achieve under 68% average compliance with 2,500+ expert-written rubrics across domain-diverse prompts.
methodology: 2,800+ hours of human labor building a rubric-based benchmark (ResearchRubrics) with a three-axis complexity framework (breadth, nesting, exploration) and human/model-based rubric-adherence evaluation protocols.
why_it_matters: Shows in detail how to build a rigorous evaluation set for deep-research/literature-search agents — query sourcing, expert rubric labeling, complexity categorization — directly answering decision 3, and the sub-68% ceiling cautions against taking reported gains at face value.
limitations: Focuses on open-ended report quality rather than literature retrieval recall specifically
Rubric-based scoring does not isolate retrieval contribution from synthesis quality
relevance_reason: A rigorously constructed benchmark for deep-research agents, central to the benchmark-construction decision question.

key_finding: On a fixed, human-verified corpus, Search-R1 with a BM25 retriever achieves only 3.86% accuracy while GPT-5 achieves 55.9%, rising to 70.1% with fewer search calls when paired with the Qwen3-Embedding-8B retriever.
methodology: Introduces BrowseComp-Plus, a fixed corpus derived from BrowseComp with human-verified supporting documents and mined hard negatives, enabling disentangled evaluation of agent versus retriever contributions.
why_it_matters: Gives exactly the baseline recall/precision ceiling decision 1 asks for — BM25 versus stronger embedding retrievers versus agent — under controlled conditions, and is already the benchmark several other shortlisted papers build directly on.
limitations: Corpus (~100K documents) is assembled from the benchmark's own queries plus mined negatives, which later work shows can inflate retrieval numbers
relevance_reason: Establishes the fixed-corpus, disentangled baseline-vs-agent methodology anchoring recall-ceiling and retrieval-method comparisons across this entire research area.

key_finding: Structured field extraction achieves 35.1% higher semantic similarity (0.655 vs 0.485, p<0.000001) than PDF-chunking RAG, with an agentic self-correction loop reaching 68.3% single-pass success and 99.0% citation accuracy.
methodology: Eight-stage ETL+RAG pipeline combining semantic search, keyword filtering, and knowledge-graph traversal with agentic self-correction and post-hoc citation verification; evaluated on 643 observations from 60 sessions applied to ozone/cardiovascular-disease literature.
why_it_matters: A concrete hybrid-retrieval architecture (semantic + keyword + KG traversal) for literature synthesis, showing structured extraction beats naive chunking — directly relevant to retrieval-architecture design choices.
limitations: Single-author work with a small evaluation set and no independent benchmark comparison
Applied to one epidemiology corpus, limiting generalization claims
relevance_reason: Directly implements the hybrid retrieval plus knowledge-graph architecture the brief asks about, in the scientific-literature-search setting itself.

key_finding: Provides a taxonomy of Deep Research agent architectures (static/dynamic workflows, single/multi-agent) and identifies benchmark limitations including restricted external-knowledge access and metric misalignment with practical DR objectives.
methodology: Systematic literature review and taxonomy of DR agent architectures, information-acquisition strategies (API vs. browser retrieval), and tool-use frameworks, with a maintained repository of DR agent research.
why_it_matters: Orients the whole scan: names the architectural building blocks and critiques the benchmarks in ways that directly shape which papers to trust for the agentic-mechanism and benchmark-construction decisions.
limitations: Narrative/taxonomic review rather than quantitative synthesis
No new empirical measurement of recall ceilings or gain attribution
relevance_reason: The main survey/roadmap synthesizing the field's architectures and benchmark critiques, useful as an orienting reference.

key_finding: DeepResearch Bench provides 100 PhD-level research tasks across 22 fields with two novel evaluation methodologies — reference-based report grading and a citation-accuracy/effective-citation-count framework — that achieve strong alignment with human judgment.
methodology: Benchmark construction: expert-crafted tasks across 22 domains, paired with reference-based adaptive-criteria grading and a citation-based retrieval-evaluation framework; open-sourced.
why_it_matters: Shows exactly how a deep-research/literature-style benchmark's query source and labeling were constructed, including a citation-accuracy metric separating retrieval quality from synthesis quality — a template other benchmarks in this scan should be checked against for decision 3.
limitations: Report-quality grading is reference-based and may not capture recall against a full literature corpus
Domain-diverse tasks are not literature-search-specific
relevance_reason: A widely-used benchmark whose construction methodology is directly what decision 3 asks the scan to assess.

key_finding: Relocating BrowseComp-Plus questions' evidence into an independently built 400B-token corpus (ClimbMix) collapses the strongest agent's evidence recall from 84.3% to 21.4% while accuracy drops only five points and search calls rise 63%.
methodology: Introduces a projection pipeline decomposing questions into atomic reasoning hops and re-grounding each hop in a benchmark-independent corpus, verified by automatic checks, an independent agent, and human review; yields 57 fully grounded questions from 830 BrowseComp-Plus test questions.
why_it_matters: Exactly the target of decision 4: a reported agentic-search gain (evidence recall) shrinks dramatically once the fixed, per-query-curated corpus is swapped for an independently assembled one, showing benchmark construction was inflating retrieval numbers.
limitations: Only 57 fully-grounded questions survive the pipeline, a small sample
Not yet validated across benchmarks beyond BrowseComp-Plus
relevance_reason: The clearest evidence in the shortlist of a reported agentic-search gain failing to hold under a less-curated corpus — exactly what decision 4 asks for.

key_finding: Adding a Retrieval-Aware Agent Controller (RAAC) using search-novelty and information-coverage signals reduces search calls by an average of 14 and improves the best-performing agent's accuracy by up to 10% (3% on average) on BrowseComp-Plus.
methodology: Analyzes reasoning trajectories across multiple deep-research agents to identify reasoning stagnation, then introduces unsupervised novelty/coverage signals and a controller module tested across a large set of DRAs.
why_it_matters: Attributes a measured gain to a specific, identifiable mechanism (retrieval-aware action selection) rather than treating the system as a black box, directly answering decision 2 with a quantified contribution.
limitations: Evaluated only on BrowseComp-Plus-style benchmarks, not literature-search corpora specifically
Average gain is modest (3%) and depends heavily on the base agent
relevance_reason: Isolates and quantifies the contribution of a specific agentic control mechanism, precisely the gain-attribution the brief asks for.

key_finding: EviReform's evidence-guided residual-query mechanism for graph retrieval exceeds the strongest baseline by up to 5.59 Recall@5 points and 4.50 F1 points on 2WikiMultiHopQA, HotpotQA, and MuSiQue.
methodology: Separates retrieval-request revision from graph evidence aggregation, forming residual queries from retrieved passages and propagating retrieval signals between propositions sharing entities.
why_it_matters: A concrete, quantified query-reformulation-plus-graph-retrieval technique — directly relevant to the retrieval/reranking method question, though tested on general multi-hop QA rather than scientific-paper citation graphs.
limitations: Evaluated on Wikipedia-based multi-hop QA datasets, not scientific-literature citation graphs
No comparison against a single-query baseline recall ceiling
relevance_reason: A query-reformulation-plus-graph-retrieval method matching the retrieval/reranking criterion, in a neighbouring but not literature-search setting.

key_finding: DynaKRAG's learned state-conditioned policy for coordinating retrieval, reformulation, and sufficiency-checking ranks first in EM/F1 across nine dataset-backbone pairs while cutting total tokens by 10.1-34.3% and retrieval calls by 15.1-43.4%.
methodology: Unified evidence-action framework with a validity layer, learned continuation gate, and learned advantage scorer, evaluated on HotpotQA, 2Wiki, MuSiQue with three LLM backbones.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates efficiency gains from learned iterative-retrieval control, background for the retrieval/reranking layer underlying agentic search, though gains are efficiency-focused rather than recall-ceiling or benchmark-construction focused.
limitations: Tested only on general multi-hop QA benchmarks, not scientific literature search
Efficiency gains reported without isolating which specific action type drives improvement
relevance_reason: A retrieval-control method for multi-hop RAG efficiency, tangential to but not squarely within the literature-search setting.

key_finding: PaperPilot-9B, which frames literature search as an executable DAG of operators (keyword search, citation expansion, filtering, scoring, reranking, evidence extraction), improves multi-turn Hit@5 from 58.0 to 77.0, MRR from 47.5 to 59.4, and nDCG@10 from 26.8 to 32.5 over a base toolset agent, while cutting workflow execution errors from 9.5% to 0%.
methodology: Trains a 9B model via supervised workflow imitation and preference optimization over controlled workflow corruptions; evaluates multi-turn scientific literature search against a Qwen3.5-9B toolset-agent baseline.
why_it_matters: The paper closest to the brief's exact system: explicit, editable workflows decomposing citation expansion, reformulation, and reranking as separately controllable operators — directly answers which specific agentic moves (decision 2) carry measured gains in a literature-search-specific setting.
limitations: Gains measured against a single toolset-agent baseline, not a pure single-query database-search baseline
9B-scale model; unclear how gains generalize to larger or different backbones
relevance_reason: The most directly on-target paper: a scientific-literature-search agent with explicit citation-expansion, reformulation, and reranking operators, quantifying each design's contribution.

key_finding: Across 26 full-text-coded autonomous research-agent systems, 83% release code but only 38% release reproducibility artifacts or report any novelty-verification method, and no system in the corpus demonstrates an externally validated in-loop oracle.
methodology: Survey screening 125 candidate AI-scientist systems, coding 26 in full across seven audit dimensions (lifecycle stage, autonomy, evaluation method, released artifacts, human-in-the-loop, novelty verification, result-selection disclosure).
why_it_matters: A reproducibility/verification audit of end-to-end AI-scientist systems (of which literature search is one lifecycle stage) — a useful caution about trusting reported capability claims, but its focus is the full research lifecycle rather than literature-search retrieval or benchmark construction specifically.
limitations: Covers the entire AI-scientist lifecycle, not literature search specifically
Abstract gives no findings on retrieval recall, agentic mechanisms, or benchmark construction relevant to this brief's core decisions
relevance_reason: Tangentially related survey on verification gaps in autonomous research agents; included for context but not central to the brief's four decision questions.

key_finding: Search-time contamination (benchmark metadata, question-context, or answer leakage via web search) inflates deep research agent benchmark performance by up to 4% across six public benchmarks.
methodology: Defines three contamination severity types and develops detection algorithms; evaluates modern deep research agents on six public benchmarks. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Directly answers decision 4: shows reported agentic gains on public benchmarks can be inflated by leaked benchmark content via web search rather than genuine retrieval/reasoning improvement, and questions cross-system comparability (decision 3).
limitations: Only quantifies up to 4% inflation, not the full picture of where gains come from
Framed around web-search deep research agents generally, not literature-search agents specifically
relevance_reason: Directly targets decision 4 (gain replication failure) by showing benchmark contamination inflates deep research agent scores.

key_finding: Citations in Agentic GraphRAG are necessary but not sufficient: removing cited evidence substantially reduces accuracy, but uncited traversal context and graph structure also shape answers.
methodology: Controlled ablation experiments isolating, removing, and masking cited/uncited graph entities in an agentic GraphRAG system. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Suggests that evaluating citation-graph traversal purely by cited-source support misses the effect of uncited traversal context, a caveat for how graph-traversal gains should be measured under decision 2.
limitations: General knowledge-graph QA setting, not specifically scientific paper citation graphs
No comparison against a single-query retrieval baseline
relevance_reason: Bears on how citation-graph traversal mechanisms should be evaluated, but in a general GraphRAG setting rather than literature search specifically.

key_finding: PaSaMaster achieves a 16.5x higher F1-score than Google Scholar and a 37.8% higher F1-score than GPT-5.2, at about 1% of the cost, while reducing source hallucination from 32.66% to zero across 38 disciplines.
methodology: Recursive self-evolving agentic retrieval system separating intent-understanding (frontier LLM) from retrieval/scoring (lightweight models); evaluated on PaSaMaster-Bench spanning 38 disciplines. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Provides a concrete recent system design (self-evolving retrieval plus planning/retrieval separation) with a large multidisciplinary benchmark quantifying gains over single-query baselines, directly informing decisions 1-3.
limitations: Abstract gives no detail on benchmark query source or relevance labeling
Self-reported comparison; no independent replication reported
relevance_reason: Directly addresses agentic mechanism attribution and baseline comparison central to the brief's core decisions.

key_finding: Across agent harnesses, grep-based retrieval generally yields higher accuracy than vector retrieval on a 116-question LongMemEval sample, though results depend strongly on harness and tool-calling style.
methodology: Two empirical experiments comparing grep vs. vector retrieval across a custom harness (Chronos) and provider-native CLIs (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI), including a distractor-density manipulation. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Shows a simple lexical baseline can beat 'fancier' retrieval inside an agent loop and that harness architecture confounds retrieval-strategy comparisons, a caution for attributing gains in agentic search benchmarks (decisions 1 and 3).
limitations: Setting is conversational memory (LongMemEval), not scientific literature search
Small sample (116 questions)
relevance_reason: Empirically shows agentic retrieval choice doesn't uniformly beat a simpler baseline, relevant to how gains should be attributed, though outside the literature-search setting.

key_finding: GraphRAG frequently underperforms vanilla RAG on many real-world tasks; GraphRAG-Bench systematically identifies the specific task conditions under which graph structure actually helps.
methodology: Introduces GraphRAG-Bench with tasks of increasing difficulty (fact retrieval, complex reasoning, summarization, creative generation) and evaluates the full GraphRAG pipeline end-to-end. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Directly tests whether graph-traversal mechanisms carry the gains agentic designs claim (decision 2) and finds they often do not, with a benchmark-construction template relevant to decision 3.
limitations: Domain is general RAG QA across generic topics, not scientific-paper citation graphs specifically
Does not isolate query reformulation or iterative crawling separately from graph structure
relevance_reason: Tests whether graph traversal (one of the brief's named agentic mechanisms) delivers real gains over vanilla retrieval and shows it often doesn't, but in a generic RAG setting rather than literature search.

key_finding: Deep Research Bench (89 multi-step web research tasks across 8 categories) shows offline 'RetroSearch' agents perform comparably to live-web agents, enabling reliable, repeatable evaluation of deep research agents over time.
methodology: Human-verified 89-task benchmark; frozen-web RetroSearch replay environment; automated trace analysis for hallucination, tool-use, and forgetting metrics. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete answer to decision 3: how to construct a benchmark for search/research agents that controls for the changing web, directly usable as a template for literature-search-agent benchmark design.
limitations: General web research tasks, not specifically scientific literature search
Modest sample of 89 task instances
relevance_reason: Provides a rigorous, replicable benchmark-construction method for deep research/search agents, directly informing decision 3.

key_finding: PaSa-7B surpasses the best Google-based baseline by 37.78% in recall@20 and 39.90% in recall@50 on RealScholarQuery, and exceeds a GPT-4o-prompted variant by 30.36% in recall and 4.25% in precision.
methodology: RL-trained LLM agent for academic paper search, trained on synthetic AutoScholarQuery (35k queries) and evaluated on the real-world RealScholarQuery benchmark.
why_it_matters: The canonical baseline-vs-agentic-gain comparison for scholarly search, establishing concrete recall numbers against single-query search baselines that later systems must be measured against (decisions 1 and 2).
limitations: Training relies on synthetic query generation, which may not fully generalize
No independent replication or alternative benchmark reported here
relevance_reason: Foundational system establishing the quantitative baseline-vs-agentic-gain comparison the brief's decisions 1 and 2 are built around.

key_finding: PaperQA2 matches or exceeds subject-matter-expert performance on literature search, summarization, and contradiction-detection tasks, identifying 2.34 +/- 1.99 contradictions per paper, 70% validated by human experts.
methodology: Rigorous human-AI comparison methodology on real-world literature research tasks; introduces the LitQA2 benchmark used to guide PaperQA2's design. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: A landmark 'superhuman' result underlying the brief's premise; its LitQA2 benchmark and human-comparison methodology are directly relevant to decision 3, though it reports no single-query baseline ceiling or mechanism attribution needed for decisions 1-2.
limitations: Contradiction-detection evaluation restricted largely to biology papers
No single-query database search baseline recall reported for direct comparison
relevance_reason: Central, highly-cited result testing the premise the brief wants scrutinized, with a benchmark and methodology directly relevant to decision 3.

key_finding: State-of-the-art embedding retrieval (59.0 nDCG@10 on MTEB) drops to 18.3 nDCG@10 on BRIGHT's reasoning-intensive queries; explicit query reasoning recovers up to 12.2 points.
methodology: 1,384 real-world reasoning-intensive queries across economics, psychology, mathematics, and coding; benchmarks retrieval models with and without explicit query reasoning. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Quantifies how low the single-query embedding-retrieval ceiling can fall on reasoning-heavy queries and shows reformulation-style reasoning recovers part of the gap, directly informing decisions 1 and 2, though in non-literature query domains.
limitations: Query domains (economics, psychology, math, coding) are not scientific-literature search specifically
Does not test citation-graph traversal or iterative crawling
relevance_reason: Provides a striking, quantified single-query baseline recall ceiling and a reformulation-style gain, relevant to decisions 1 and 2, in a neighbouring retrieval-benchmark setting.

key_finding: LAB-Bench, a 2,400+ multiple-choice benchmark, assesses literature recall/reasoning, figure interpretation, database navigation, and sequence manipulation in biology research against human expert performance.
methodology: Multiple-choice benchmark construction across several practical biology-research capability categories, comparing frontier LLM performance to human experts. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Offers one benchmark-construction approach relevant to decision 3, but only a fraction of its scope is literature search per se, limiting how much it can inform the brief's core questions.
limitations: Most of the benchmark covers non-literature-search biology tasks (DNA/protein manipulation, figure interpretation)
MCQ format doesn't capture open-ended retrieval recall/precision the way search tasks do
relevance_reason: Partial overlap with benchmark-construction decision 3 via its literature-recall component, but mostly outside literature-search-agent scope.

key_finding: Crase, using bounded 1.5-hop citation-graph expansion with entailment-based pruning and recency-aware random-walk ranking, outperforms deep research agents built on proprietary models by up to 3x recall@50 at roughly a third of the cost on LitSearch and a further benchmark over a 500K-paper arXiv corpus.
methodology: Single seed-paper search, fixed 1.5-hop citation expansion, entailment-based edge pruning, recency-aware random-walk ranking; evaluated on LitSearch plus one further benchmark. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Attributes a measured recall gain to a specific, bounded citation-graph-traversal mechanism rather than an open-ended agent loop, and shows this beats costlier open-ended deep-research agents, exactly the mechanism-attribution evidence decision 2 needs.
limitations: Evaluated on only LitSearch plus one further benchmark
Bounded to 1.5-hop neighborhoods, may miss longer-range citation structure
relevance_reason: The clearest example here of attributing a measured recall gain to a specific, named agentic mechanism (bounded citation-graph traversal) rather than an undifferentiated agent system.

key_finding: DAS, a stateful agentic survey-generation framework built on a 2M-paper metadata lake, achieves the highest average score (4.34 vs. 4.03 for the strongest competitor) across 30 topics on DAS-Bench/DAS-Eval, preferred by blinded experts on 27/30 topics over Naive RAG.
methodology: Stateful closed-loop framework separating reusable paper analysis from topic-specific manuscript construction; introduces DAS-Bench (30 topics) and DAS-Eval (16 criteria). Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Shares agentic literature-organization and citation-planning machinery with search agents, giving a data point on evidence-grounded citation planning at scale, but its evaluation targets survey-writing quality rather than search recall/precision (decisions 1, 2).
limitations: Evaluation targets survey-writing quality, not search recall/precision directly
No comparison to single-query database search baseline
relevance_reason: Adjacent literature-organization/citation-planning system, but downstream of the search task the brief centers on.
